scenes.narration: Meet Pihu. This morning at assembly, Teacher Sara holds up a big shiny shield and says: 'Every child in India carries an invisible shield like this one. It is called a RIGHT. It keeps you safe, lets you learn and play, and makes sure you are treated fairly.' Pihu whispers: 'Even me?' What is the true answer?

choices.text: Yes! Every single child has these shields — Pihu, you, everyone.
choices.feedback: Exactly right. Rights are not prizes you win or gifts only some children get. Every child has them from the day they are born, no matter what. You matter, always.

choices.text: Only children with the best marks get shields.
choices.feedback: No. Rights have nothing to do with marks, money, or being the fastest runner. EVERY child carries the same invisible shields — including you. Nothing can change that.

scenes.narration: At lunch, a new girl named Amaira sits alone. She speaks a different language and wears different clothes. A boy laughs: 'She can't play with us, she is not like us.' Pihu remembers the shield talk. What is true?

choices.text: Amaira has the exact same shields. She gets the same chance to play, learn, and be respected.
choices.feedback: Yes! Being equal means exactly this: different language, different food, different clothes — same rights, same respect. Pihu invites Amaira to play, and lunchtime becomes more fun for everyone.

choices.text: Children who seem different have smaller shields.
choices.feedback: No. There is no such thing as a smaller shield. No child can be treated as less because of how they look, talk, pray, or where they come from. Same rights. Same respect. Every time.
Shields work everywhere — home, school, the playground, the whole country! Every child, everywhere in India, carries them all day, every day.

scenes.narration: In class, Teacher Sara asks: 'Who can tell me what your invisible shields protect?' Hands fly up. Pihu thinks hard. Which answer should Pihu give?

choices.text: My safety, my learning, my playtime, and being treated with respect.
choices.feedback: Perfect. That is what rights protect: your body being safe, your chance to go to school, your time to play and rest, and being treated like you matter — because you do.

choices.text: They make sure I always win games.
choices.feedback: Not quite! Rights are not about winning or getting everything you wish for. They protect the BIG things: being safe, learning, playing, and being respected. Those belong to you no matter who wins the game.

scenes.narration: Walking home, Pihu's little cousin asks: 'What if someone makes a child feel small, scared, or unsafe? What happens to the shield?' Pihu smiles: 'The shield never breaks. And a child never has to hold it alone.' What is the BEST thing a child can do then?

choices.text: Tell a trusted grown-up, like Amma, Papa, or a teacher — and remember Childline 1098, a free phone friend for children.
choices.feedback: Exactly right. When something feels wrong, telling a trusted grown-up is strong and brave. And any child in India can call 1098 for free, day or night. You matter, your safety matters, and help is always there.

choices.text: Hide the problem and hope it goes away.
choices.feedback: Hiding a problem does not make it smaller. Telling a trusted grown-up does. And Childline 1098 is always there, free, for any child. Asking for help is never wrong — you matter too much for that.

quizQuestions.question: Who has rights — the invisible shields that keep children safe and respected?
quizQuestions.explanation: Every child is born with rights. No mark sheet, no amount of money, nothing can take them away.

quizQuestions.question: A new classmate speaks a different language. How do her rights compare to yours?
options: She has none until she learns our language
quizQuestions.explanation: Same rights, same respect, always. No child can be treated as less for language, clothes, food, or where they come from.

quizQuestions.question: Someone makes a child feel scared or small. What is the strongest thing to do?
options: Tell a trusted grown-up, or call Childline 1098
Wait until the child grows up
quizQuestions.explanation: Telling is brave and strong. Trusted grown-ups can help, and Childline 1098 is free for any child, any time, day or night.
